newsitem.title: LEBANON: Judge's resignation halts Lebanese vote appeals.
newsitem.headline: Judge's resignation halts Lebanese vote appeals.

text.p: The head of Lebanon's Constitutional Council resigned on Thursday amid reports it was facing heavy political pressure over a score of appeals against the results of last year's parliamentary elections.

"I officially announce my resignation from the presidency and membership of the council," Judge Wajdi al-Mallat said in a letter read to parliament by Speaker Nabih Berri. He did not read out a document Mallat attached giving his reasons.
However, parliamentary deputies and legal sources said the judges had been under pressure for two weeks from top political figures concerning 19 appeals by losing election candidates.

The 10-judge court established in 1994 is the first independent body empowered to rule on Lebanese elections. The appeals are the first it has heard and it has been studying 40,000 documents of evidence for the past six months.
Most appelants were opponents of the pro-Syrian government whose supporters swept to victory in the 128-seat parliament amid allegations of intimidation and other abuses.
The court's decisions had been expected in a few days, but Mallat told Reuters it was now unable to act until parliament appointed a new member.
Political analysts said the resignation confronted Lebanon with a major constitutional test.
"If the Constitutional Council cannot act without some unanimity and independence then the whole thing is a fig leaf," a Beirut analyst who asked not to be identified told Reuters.
Eighteen losing candidates have asked the court to overturn results and declare them the winners. Another asked the court to cancel the entire election.
After Berri read Mallat's letter to parliament, opposition deputy Boutros Harb said he resigned due to political pressure.
"It is obvious the Constitutional Council is being subjected to pressures and the issue should not be dealt with lightly. We want to know who is pressuring the council," he said.
Opposition deputy Zaher al-Khatib said: "I have information that the government or its head is interfering with the work of the council."
"What is this talk? It is unacceptable," billionaire Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri retorted angrily.
Legal sources told Reuters the 10-member court was split over the appeals as well as being under political pressure.

It was ready to overturn three results and replace winners with defeated appelants, the sources said. But these involved only mistakes in vote-counting and the government was pressuring the court to limit rulings in favour of the appeals to these cases, the sources said.
"This would restrict the court to being a sort of accounting bureau only able to deal with cases involving mistakes in adding and subtracting," a lawyer told Reuters.

However, the court was divided over three appeals against civil servants or members of official institutions who won election despite failing to resign their posts in the prescribed period before the election.
The sources said records were falsified to show they quit in time, but a decision against them would trigger criminal charges as well as loss of their seats in parliament.
At least one judge wanted the court to overturn all election results in which it found abuses and order new polls. However, the sources said the court was unlikely to order re-runs.
